issues.description: The problem statement (and UML) requires addGuestStudents(int, String) — i.e. a method that accepts an int and a String reason — but the solution implements addGuestStudents(int) with only a single int parameter. This parameter mismatch will confuse students about the required method signature and can cause tests or instructions that expect the (int, String) overload to fail.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the method signatures consistent. Either (A) update the solution and template to implement addGuestStudents(int numberOfNewGuestStudents, String reason) — e.g. add the String parameter and (optionally) record or log the reason while updating numberOfGuestStudents — or (B) update the problem statement and UML to require addGuestStudents(int) only. Prefer option A to match the current specification in the problem statement.

issues.description: The problem statement and UML require a method addGuestStudents(int, String) (an int plus a String reason). The solution implements addGuestStudents(int) with a single int parameter (named numberOfNewGuestStudents) and no String parameter. This mismatch in the method signature (parameter count and types) creates a mapping confusion: students expect to implement or use a two-parameter method with a reason String, but the provided solution/template code uses a different signature.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the method signature across artifacts to match the problem statement. Change the implementation and template to declare addGuestStudents(int numberOfNewGuestStudents, String reason) (or similar parameter names) so the method accepts both the new guest count and the reason. Ensure the method is documented/used consistently in tests and examples.
